title: Geomagnetic storms may show northern lights in Metro Vancouver as storms clear
excerpt: You may have more than one chance to view the colourful display in the Lower Mainland.
content:
You may have more than one chance to view the colourful display in the Lower Mainland.

Locals might see some colourful dancing lights this week due to active solar winds. 

The Metro Vancouver weather forecast calls for active storms through Thursday (Nov. 26), but Friday's forecast includes clearing skies overnight Friday. If the prediction pans out, Mother Nature may paint the heavens with purple and green hues. 

  • Related: 'Aurora spotted!' Metro Vancouverites capture photos of northern lights dancing

Currently, a coronal hole on the Sun's equator is expected to increase solar wind speed toward our planet, increasing the likelihood of geomagnetic storms, according to LiveScience.com. 

The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration's Space Weather Prediction Center hasn't issued a geomagnetic storm watch yet. It only issues one within three days of the event. But it notes that "geomagnetic field activity is likely to range from quiet to G1 (Minor) geomagnetic storm levels" on Friday (Nov. 27) and again on Dec. 4.

Wednesday and Saturday may also see more active space conditions, although geomagnetic storms aren't expected, according to the update.

Metro Vancouver weather forecast: Possible northern lights viewing opportunities

The University of Alaska Fairbanks (UAF) expects "high aurora activity" on Friday, with displays possible "overhead from locations such as Inuvik, Yellowknife, Rankin and Iqaluit, Canada, to Juneau, Alaska, Edmonton, Winnipeg, Thunder Bay and Sept-Iles, Canada; and may be visible low on the horizon from Seattle, Des Moines, Chicago, Cleveland and Boston, U.S.A., and Halifax, Canada."

The university's online aurora monitor map shows what regions the aurora's green glow will likely reach, and other areas where it is less likely. Additionally, a brief description below the map shows the aurora activity on that particular day.

Saturday may offer another potential viewing, with "active aurora activity" and displays possibly low on the horizon in Vancouver. However, the aurora will be less active than on Friday, meaning viewing might not be as good. 

The aurora borealis often appears as a milky manifestation moving in the night sky rather than vibrant hues. While a camera with a long exposure is useful for capturing the vibrancy of the aurora, the newest smartphones have a darklight mode that will also capture colours the human eye can't see at night.
